title: Ultra-high-distance quantum memories from amplified qLDPC codes
authors: Zijian Liang, Boren Gu, Yu-An Chen, Jens Eisert, Zongyuan Wang
abstract: A large code distance does not by itself guarantee a well-protected quantum memory, as faults during syndrome extraction can propagate into correlated data errors. Certifying circuit distance becomes demanding as circuits grow. In this work, we introduce distance amplifiers, a modular approach to increasing both code distance and certified circuit-level protection in quantum low-density parity-check codes. The construction tensors a base code with an amplifier, adapting their syndrome-extraction circuits to the amplified code. To certify the resulting memory, we develop a fault-response certificate that yields rigorous lower bounds on circuit distance. Suitable gate ordering and flag qubits control correlated errors, allowing us to establish explicit conditions under which the amplified circuit distance equals the product of the constituent circuit distances. We prove this multiplicative relation for three types of amplifiers: the flagged $[[4,2,2]]$, hypergraph-product, and rotated surface codes. The certificate extends recursively, so the circuit distance multiplies exactly at every amplification step. For example, four successive applications of the flagged $[[4,2,2]]$ amplifier to a $[[18,4,4]]$ seed yield a $[[13320,64,64]]$ code with the circuit distance $d_{\mathrm{circ}} \geq 48$ and check weights $w \leq 14$. We further show how individual logical qubits can be tracked explicitly through amplification. By enabling high-distance quantum memories to be built and certified from smaller building blocks, our framework offers a systematic route toward scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing.
summary: This work presents a novel 'distance amplifier' technique to construct quantum memories with exponentially increasing fault tolerance. By developing a fault-response certificate, the authors prove that the circuit distance of the resulting qLDPC code multiplies at each amplification step. This offers a systematic and scalable route toward fault-tolerant quantum computing.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of building quantum memories with sufficiently high fault tolerance, recognizing that simple code distance is insufficient due to error propagation during syndrome extraction.
main_result: They introduce 'distance amplifiers' that allow for the modular, recursive construction of qLDPC codes, proving a multiplicative relationship for the certified circuit distance across amplification steps.
method: The authors develop a 'fault-response certificate' and use a modular tensor-product approach to combine base codes with amplifiers, rigorously bounding the circuit distance.
model_or_system: The system is a quantum memory encoded using quantum Low-Density Parity-Check (qLDPC) codes. The structure is built by tensoring a base code with an amplifier code, forming an amplified code T = Q $\otimes$ A.
key_observables: Certified circuit distance ($d_{	ext{circ}}$), code parameters ($e_n, e_k$), and the logical error rate per round ($p_L$).
important_parameters: The multiplicative gain factor ($\alpha_P$) achieved by the amplifier, and the physical error probability ($p$).
main_assumptions: The multiplicative property of the circuit distance holds when the seed certificate is attained, and the analysis relies on bounding fault costs by summing local responses.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate recursive amplification structures and the staged joint syndrome extraction process, detailing error propagation and logical data responses.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first identifying the limitations of simple distance metrics, then introducing the distance amplifier framework, proving the multiplicative circuit distance bound for specific amplifiers, and finally demonstrating the recursive application to build high-distance codes.
why_interesting: The rigorous, systematic framework for building fault-tolerant quantum memories by multiplying protection levels is highly relevant for designing scalable quantum computation architectures.
